paragraph: The very next day Ravana rode out in his chariot drawn by four donkeys, its dazzle lighting up the four directions. He stopped at the hermitage of Maricha. Welcoming him with great affection Maricha asked Ravana, "Your sudden visit makes me anxious, is all well with the Rakshasa world? And Ravana said, "Rama has effortlessly wiped out my indomitable army and those that command it. I seek your help in abducting his wife." Maricha was shocked. He wanted to dissuade Ravana from his mission and said, "Only your enemy would advise you this. He goads you to commit the unpardonable to hasten your destruction and that of the rakshasas. He is your enemy who pretending friendship counsels you to abduct Sita. Born of the noble Ikshvaku race and endowed with the strength of an elephant, Rama's powers have no compare. If provoked, his fury will spell your doom. Be wise, shed your anger, go back home to be happy in the company of your wives and Rama will be happy in the forest with Sita. Ravana heeding Maricha's counsel returned to Lanka.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Ravana, despite being advised by Akampana to abduct Sita, seeks further counsel from Maricha. He explicitly states his intention to abduct Sita. Maricha, having firsthand experience of Rama's power, is horrified and attempts to dissuade Ravana by warning him of Rama's immense strength and the catastrophic consequences of such an action, appealing to his wisdom and self-preservation.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights the importance of seeking and heeding wise counsel, especially when contemplating a dangerous or immoral act. Maricha acts as a voice of reason, demonstrating foresight and courage in speaking truth to power, even to a formidable figure like Ravana. It also shows that even those on the 'wrong' side can recognize and warn against self-destructive paths. For a brief moment, good counsel prevails over ego and desire.
Outcome/Resolution: Maricha successfully dissuades Ravana, at least temporarily, from his plan to abduct Sita by vividly describing Rama's power and the devastating consequences. Ravana, convinced by Maricha's sincere and fearful warning, returns to Lanka without attempting the abduction.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Adharma (Unrighteous Conduct - Ravana's intent to abduct)
Viveka (Discernment - Maricha's ability to distinguish right from wrong)
Moha (Delusion - Ravana's initial persistence despite warnings)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Spiritually, this passage underscores the critical role of wise counsel (Buddhi and Viveka) in guiding one away from the path of Adharma. Maricha, having experienced Rama's power, attempts to steer Ravana towards Dharma by urging him to 'shed his anger' and abandon his unrighteous intent stemming from Kama. For a fleeting moment, Ravana heeds this righteous advice, demonstrating that even those deeply entrenched in Moha can be temporarily swayed by truth, albeit his true Ahamkara and Lobha would eventually reassert themselves.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Ravana, despite his initial resolve, shows a momentary capacity for emotional regulation and heeding wise counsel as he 'sheds his anger' and returns to Lanka. Maricha, on the other hand, exhibits strong stress management and courage by directly confronting Ravana's dangerous intentions with a clear, rational warning, appealing to Ravana's self-preservation and highlighting the dangers of his unchecked ego and anger. Maricha's anxiety ('Your sudden visit makes me anxious') shows his personal fear but also his commitment to preventing a catastrophe.
